name: Christian left
summary: The Christian left reads the gospel as a call to social justice: care for the poor and oppressed, criticism of concentrated wealth, support for welfare and labor, peace-making and, in many strands, a consistent defence of life that also opposes capital punishment. It is a loose family of movements rather than one doctrine, and it divides on sexual ethics, abortion, and how far to adopt socialism or Marxist analysis.

abortion-legal.rationale: Stead (vol. 1, Introduction, pp. xi-xii) lists among social Christianity's achievements that it 'banned with ascending execration' marital incontinence, 'race-suicide', 'pre-natal murder' and infanticide.

ban-interest.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, p. 453) calls the medieval Church's prohibition of usury, 'however mistaken it may seem to us', a protection to debtors against the unscrupulous creditor, treating the ban as mistaken rather than as a rule to restore.

class-collaboration.rationale: Laun (ch. III, pp. 79-80, on Maurice, Kingsley and Ludlow) says brotherhood, not competition and class war, is what Christianity and the Christian Socialists stood for, and (Introduction, pp. 3-4) that class war only substitutes one oppressor class for another, while only Christianity overcomes selfishness.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The social gospel's 1908 social creed affirmed labor's right to unionize and bargain collectively.

death-penalty.rationale: Citizendium says the Christian left's valuing of human life usually implies opposition to capital punishment, and Dissent's Catholic example opposes it morally; the sources hedge, so the answer is moderate.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Lux Mundi's essay on Christianity and Politics (essay XI, pp. 446-449) sets out St Paul's teaching that 'all power is of Divine origin' and calls it the theological ground of civil authority, adding that 'all just power is of God' and so a trust for the good of others.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Stead (vol. 1, ch. on the New Testament, p. 37) reads the apostolic rule that the labourer 'must be the first to partake of the fruits' as meaning 'the living wage of the labourer must be the first charge upon production'.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Social Christianity held that relying only on supply and demand to allocate resources and set wages was un-Christian.

more-religion-public.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, p. 458) says that in the best ordering religion would be 'the foundation and the coping stone of national life' and the State given a distinctly Christian character.

national-church-status.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, pp. 455-458) takes as the most perfect ordering a Church and State united and mutually supporting, and weighs disestablishment only as an expedient, with the Church in England as the historical Church of the nation.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, pp. 446-451) puts 'first and foremost' the duty of obedience to duly constituted civil authority for conscience' sake, with the same sanctions as the most sacred claims, limited only where commands are contrary to virtue or religion.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Gore's Sermon on the Mount (ch. IV, on the law of divorce, pp. 73-75) holds marriage indissoluble by the law of Christ, which no parliament can alter, and says remarried divorcees cannot be regarded as married; Stead (vol. 1, Introduction, p. xi) likewise lists that Christianity 'has forbidden Divorce'.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Stead (vol. 1, Introduction, p. xii) says Christianity 'reminded the rich of the perils that attend their riches' and 'demanded from them large liberality to the poor'.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: Stead (vol. 1, Introduction, p. xi) counts it among social Christianity's achievements that it laid down its own marriage laws and 'doomed polygamy'.

property-fundamental.rationale: Laun (ch. III, note 45) says the COPEC idea of property is a compromise in which personal property is limited by and depends on the community's rights, and Stead (vol. 1, Introduction, p. xii) says Christianity laid down 'severe laws for property' and rebuked selfish accumulation, though without abolishing it. Lux Mundi (essay XI, p. 451) says Christianity is not pledged to any particular form of property, which is secondary, a means and not an end.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Stead (vol. 1, Introduction, p. xii) says Christianity has declared all wealth 'a trust from God to be used for His ends', with 'severe laws for property'; Laun (ch. III, note 45) says the COPEC report on industry and property makes the right to personal property depend on the property rights of the community. Lux Mundi (essay XI, p. 451) adds that if there is private property its true character as a trust shall be recognised.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Social gospel leaders Gladden and Rauschenbusch denounced racial inequality and lynching and extended the brotherhood of man to African Americans.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Lux Mundi's preface, by its editor Gore, says the age brings 'new needs, new points of view, new questions' and that 'theology must take a new development', needing 'some general restatement of its claim and meaning', while keeping the Creed (Preface to the first edition).

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, pp. 449-451) gives as Christian teaching the right, 'in certain extreme cases' almost a duty, of resistance to the arbitrary or unconstitutional extension of authority, and says the Divine right of princes and non-resistance misrepresented the Church's tradition.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Gore's essay 'The Holy Spirit and Inspiration' in Lux Mundi (essay VIII, pp. 353-354) denies that inspiration means a miraculous communication of facts, says inspired writers stay within the knowledge of their time, and holds that inspiration is consistent with an 'idealizing element' in the Old Testament history.

separate-church-state.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, pp. 456-458) weighs disestablishment ('a free Church in a free State') as one expedient course but says the most perfect ordering would have Church and State as two parts of one whole, with the State given a Christian character.

social-market-economy.rationale: Social gospel advocates backed the labor movement and an interventionist welfare state against laissez-faire capitalism.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, pp. 448-450) says power is a trust and a ministry, that a government aiming at anything but the common good is a tyranny, and that the Divine right of princes taught by the Caroline divines was 'a fatal error' untrue to the Church's tradition.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, pp. 455-456) argues that the subordination of the Church to the State has led to the secularization of the Church and a loss of spiritual authority to reprove social sins.

total-state.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, p. 455) says its argument shows 'the incompleteness and inevitable limitations of the State' as a moral guide of social life, which the Church's own moral and spiritual work must supplement.

unions-good.rationale: Stead (vol. 2, ch. 5, 'Christian Influence on Organized Labour', pp. 175-179) presents the organized labour movement as led and commended by Christians such as Cardinal Manning and Keir Hardie, as part of social Christianity's record.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Citizendium reports the Christian left's view that providing health care is a moral imperative, shown in its coalition campaign for health reform.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Lux Mundi (essay XI, pp. 449-451) states the duty of disobedience when civil authority commands something contrary to virtue or religion, and that subjects are not bound to obey a ruler acting outside his rights.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Laun (p. 80) quotes Kingsley's sermon: all systems of society which favour 'the accumulation of capital in a few hands', reduce the masses to 'serfs and day-labourers' or deny them 'a permanent stake in the commonwealth' are condemned by the Lord's words.

women-suffrage.rationale: Stead describes the demand for votes for women as pressed by Christian women (Frances Willard, Josephine Butler, Catharine Booth) from conviction that the principle is 'right and just' and credits their religious following with converting the electorate (vol. 2, pp. 209-210).

scope: The Christian left as the defining sources present it under the names social Christianity / Christian social movement: the tradition that reads the gospel as a social message, against religious individualism, and applies the Kingdom of Christ to poverty, labour and economic life. Stead (The Story of Social Christianity, 1924) and Laun (Social Christianity in England, 1929) trace it from Wesley through F. D. Maurice, Ludlow and the Christian Socialists of 1848-54, the Christian Social Union (Holland, Gore, Westcott, 1889) and Lux Mundi's incarnational theology to COPEC; the Dissent and Wikipedia accounts carry it to the modern Christian left against the religious right, with its consistent-life strand. It covers Christian socialism, the social gospel and liberation theology only as far as these sources tie them to it, and it excludes the religious right, apolitical piety and non-Christian socialism. It is a loose family, not one doctrine; where the strands divide (sexual ethics, abortion, socialism) the sources split.
